ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRINCIPLES__Acu:
Overview — The Decisive Fork: Upper vs Lower

The fork that governs the entire workup = upper vs lower, divided by the ligament of Treitz:

Upper GI Bleed

Oesophagus, stomach or duodenum (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). → triaged to endoscopy (OGD).

Lower GI Bleed

Below the ligament of Treitz. → triaged to imaging / colonoscopy.

SAFETY RULE: a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large fresh PR bleed has an upper GI bleed until proven otherwise (a brisk upper bleed transits fast and presents as fresh rectal blood).
VOCABULARY: haematemesis / “coffee-ground” vomit + melaena → upper; haematochezia (fresh PR blood) → usually lower.

Cross-ref: cirrhosis / varices (the variceal cause), peptic ulcer, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, shock (resuscitation).

Two Universal First Principles (before you localise)
Resuscitate First (A–E)

Unstable bleeds need urgent resuscitation, wide-bore IV access and blood products until stable; activate the major haemorrhage protocol. Use a restrictive transfusion strategy — transfuse red cells for Hb <70 g/L (target 70–90 g/L) unless there is massive haemorrhage or haemodynamic instability (NICE). In suspected variceal bleeding take particular care not to over-transfuse: raising the Hb much above 80 g/L increases portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding. Correcting coagulopathy: platelets if actively bleeding with a count below 50; for warfarin, prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K (vitamin K alone is too slow); for a DOAC, stop it and discuss with haematology. Continue low-dose aspirin taken for secondary cardiovascular prevention once haemostasis has been achieved (NICE) — stop other NSAIDs.

The FBC Trap

Acute bleeds may NOT initially show anaemia — Hb concentration lags (takes time to haemodilute), so a normal Hb never reassures in an acute bleed.

Unstable large PR bleed = upper GI bleed until proven otherwise.
Hb may be normal initially (lags); raised urea:creatinine ratio → upper source (digested blood).

Variceal: terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics + banding (oesophageal) or cyanoacrylate glue (gastric).

Management (resuscitate → endoscopy → cause-specific)
Non-variceal
  • Endoscopic haemostasis — clips or thermal coagulation.
  • PPI AFTER endoscopy, not before (NICE) — then IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h post-haemostasis).
Variceal (cross-ref cirrhosis)
  • The three-part bundle: terlipressin IV + prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics, both at presentation, + urgent endoscopic therapy — band ligation for oesophageal varices, injection of cyanoacrylate glue for gastric varices (NICE). TIPS if bleeding is not controlled endoscopically.

If endoscopy fails: CT mesenteric angiography to identify / control the source → guide embolisation.

Diverticulosis is the commonest cause; diverticular bleeds are often painless, but bleeds from diverticulitis can be painful.
Angiodysplasia (high-yield vascular cause)
Angiodysplasia
  • The most common vascular abnormality of the GI tract; AVMs forming most often in the caecum and ascending colon; an important cause of obscure and small-bowel bleeding, particularly in older patients.
  • Presents as painless occult / recurrent PR bleeding; usually stops spontaneously but frequently recurs.
  • Associations: aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome), chronic renal failure, von Willebrand disease.
  • Managed with argon plasma coagulation (APC); capsule endoscopy preferred for small-bowel lesions.
📷 Image placeholder — angiodysplasia at colonoscopy — a flat, bright-red spider-like or fern-like cluster of ectatic mucosal vessels in the caecum/ascending colon, treated with argon plasma coagulation
Clinical Features & Assessment
  • Haematochezia (fresh / maroon PR blood); painless suggests diverticular / angiodysplasia, painful suggests colitis / ischaemia. Melaena is black, tarry, sticky and offensive-smelling — distinguish it from the dry, matt-black, non-offensive stool of oral iron or bismuth, which is not a bleed.
  • All patients need a DRE + proctoscopy (exclude a bedside-treatable anorectal source — haemorrhoids).
  • Risk factors for adverse outcome: haemodynamic instability, ongoing haematochezia, age >60, creatinine >150, significant comorbidities.
  • Oakland score: stratifies whether outpatient management is feasible (age, sex, previous LGIB admissions, PR findings, HR, SBP, Hb). A score of 8 or less identifies patients who can be discharged for outpatient investigation (BSG).
Investigations — the stability-driven imaging fork

Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFT, clotting and Group & Save as a minimum; stool cultures to exclude infective causes.

Stable (~80%)

Mild & self-limiting → colonoscopy once stable + bowel-prepped (diagnostic + therapeutic).

Unstable

Resuscitate + correct coagulopathy + major haemorrhage protocol. Exclude an upper source first with OGD if the history suggests one (a brisk upper bleed can present as fresh PR blood), then urgent CT angiogram BEFORE any endoscopic therapy → permits IR embolisation.

📷 Image placeholder — CT mesenteric angiography of active GI bleeding — a blush of contrast extravasating into the bowel lumen, localising the bleeding point to guide interventional-radiology embolisation
If colonoscopy is negative: do an OGD to look for an upper source; if still inconclusive → capsule endoscopy or RBC scintigraphy.
Management
~80% settle spontaneously — stable, low-risk young patients in whom bleeding has stopped can be discharged for outpatient investigation.
  • Endoscopic therapy (clips, thermal, APC for angiodysplasia, band ligation).
  • IR embolisation (via CT angiogram) for ongoing bleeding not controlled endoscopically.
  • Surgery = last resort (unstable despite resuscitation, or failed endoscopic / IR control).

Investigations
  • Urine dip + MC&S — interpret with caution: sterile pyuria and haematuria occur in appendicitis and pelvic inflammation, and a positive dip does not exclude a surgical cause (do not use dipstick to diagnose UTI in the over-65s). Pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age, whatever the contraception or period history
  • ECG — exclude MI as epigastric pain cause
  • ABG/VBG — ↑ lactate = ischaemia; metabolic alkalosis = vomiting
  • FBC (↓Hb / ↑WCC), U&E, LFT, CRP, amylase or lipase (lipase preferred where available; >3× ULN supports pancreatitis, but lesser rises occur in perforation, bowel ischaemia and ruptured ectopic, and it can be normal in a late presentation), INR, calcium
  • Erect CXR — free air under the diaphragm supports perforation, but a normal film does not exclude it
  • CT abdo/pelvis — perforation, obstruction, ischaemia
  • USS — biliary tree, renal tract, uterus/adnexa
Initial Management Bundle
  • A–E; alert seniors early in the unwell patient
  • NBM if surgery likely or obstruction
  • NG tube if obstruction
  • IV fluids if hypovolaemia
  • IV antibiotics if infection/sepsis — score NEWS2 and screen for sepsis in every acute abdomen; take blood cultures and lactate first, and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour in high-risk sepsis. Antibiotics do not treat the source: escalate in parallel, because source control (theatre or drainage) is the definitive treatment
  • Analgesia early and titrated (IV morphine with an anti-emetic) — do not withhold opioids for fear of "masking signs"; early analgesia does not obscure the diagnosis or delay the decision to operate
  • VTE assessment + LMWH prophylaxis

Overview

Inflammation of the appendix — a blind-ended tube from the caecum where the three taeniae coli converge. Peak age teens–20s (second decade); children are the can't-miss high-risk group (atypical presentation + high perforation risk).

The decisive cascade: Luminal obstruction → trapped secretions → infection & inflammation → gangrene → rupture → peritonitis. The timeline drives urgency.
Causes of luminal obstruction
  • Faecolith — compacted faecal stone (classic)
  • Lymphoid hyperplasia — commoner in younger patients (post-viral)
  • Undigested seeds / impacted stool
  • Caecal tumour — the can't-miss cause in older patients
Cross-references
  • Acute abdomen (RIF pain workup)
  • Meckel's diverticulum (found at operation if appendix normal)
  • Mesenteric adenitis (paediatric mimic)
  • Gynae / urological RIF differentials
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — McBurney's point — two-thirds of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine, the surface marking of maximal tenderness in appendicitis
Cardinal pain pattern: Starts central / peri-umbilical (dull, poorly localised — visceral midgut pain) → migrates to RIF (sharp, well localised — parietal peritoneal inflammation). Worse on coughing / speed bumps.
Symptoms
  • Pain — central → RIF migration (key feature)
  • Vomiting after pain (pain-first = appendicitis order; vomiting-first = gastroenteritis)
  • Anorexia, nausea
  • Constipation > diarrhoea; pelvic appendicitis → rectal irritation / loose stool
Examination findings
  • McBurney's point tenderness
  • Percussion tenderness and cough tenderness (preferred to eliciting rebound — kinder and no less useful) with guarding → peritonism
  • RIF mass → appendiceal abscess
  • Sepsis signs in severe cases (tachycardia, hypotension)
  • Rovsing's sign — LIF palpation → RIF pain
  • Psoas sign — RIF pain on right hip extension → retrocaecal appendix
Children — atypical & high-risk: Often present with diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, or left-sided pain. Examine GI, urinary AND genitals in all boys (exclude testicular torsion). Child <6 years with symptoms >48 hours = high risk of having already perforated → urgent senior surgical review. Active observation with serial examination is for children with a short history and equivocal findings, not for this group.
Differentials
Adults (RIF pain)
  • Gynaecological — ovarian torsion (time-critical; a negative pregnancy test does not exclude it), ovarian cyst rupture, ectopic pregnancy, PID
  • Renal — ureteric colic, UTI, pyelonephritis
  • GI — Crohn's, Meckel's diverticulum, diverticular disease
  • Urological — testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis
Paediatric differentials
  • Mesenteric adenitis — inflamed mesenteric nodes, often post-URTI/tonsillitis; commonest paediatric mimic
  • Gastroenteritis, constipation
  • Intussusception, UTI
  • Testicular torsion (boys)
💡 Normal appendix at operation? Inspect the distal ileum for an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum — a congenital blind-ended diverticulum ~60 cm from the ileocaecal valve that can inflame, rupture, or cause volvulus/intussusception.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — CT of acute appendicitis — a dilated, thick-walled, fluid-filled appendix (>6 mm) with surrounding fat stranding, sometimes containing an appendicolith
Appendicitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis — but imaging is used increasingly in UK practice because operating on clinical grounds alone leaves a high negative appendicectomy rate, highest in women of childbearing age. A classical history with localised RIF peritonism and raised inflammatory markers may go straight to theatre; image before operating if the presentation is atypical or equivocal, and in particular in women of childbearing age, children, older patients and pregnancy.
Alvarado score (MANTRELS, /10): a clinical scoring aid — Migration of pain, Anorexia, Nausea/vomiting, Tenderness RIF (2), Rebound, Elevated temperature, Leucocytosis (2), Shift (neutrophilia). ≥7 supports appendicitis; ≤3 makes it unlikely. Supports — not replaces — clinical judgement.
🩸
FBC + CRP + G&S
Neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis; ↑ CRP. G&S if surgical intervention planned.
🔬
Urine dip + pregnancy test
Urinalysis to exclude renal/urological causes. A urine pregnancy test is mandatory in every woman of childbearing age before any decision to operate — a negative test excludes ectopic pregnancy. If positive, urgent gynaecological assessment and pelvic ultrasound are needed. Serum hCG is used where the urine test is equivocal or quantification is needed.
📷
USS / CT (if equivocal)
In women, ultrasound first: transabdominal graded-compression USS to assess the appendix, plus pelvic/transvaginal USS to assess the adnexa (torsion, cyst accident, tubo-ovarian pathology). USS preferred over CT in children (avoid radiation). CT if the diagnosis remains unclear. In pregnancy, USS first and CT avoided (fetal radiation) — non-contrast MRI is the next step if USS is inconclusive. A non-visualised appendix on USS does not exclude appendicitis — if clinical suspicion persists, proceed to further imaging or surgical review.
Management
Surgical (gold standard)
  • Initial management first — A–E assessment, IV access, bloods, IV fluids, nil by mouth, antiemetics, VTE assessment and analgesia (opioids do not mask the signs — do not withhold). If there is sepsis or peritonitis, give IV antibiotics immediately rather than waiting for theatre.
  • Laparoscopic appendicectomy — gold standard; inspect whole abdomen for other pathology
  • Pregnancy — laparoscopic appendicectomy is now considered safe in all trimesters (RCOG) and is increasingly preferred; an open/muscle-splitting (Lanz) approach remains an alternative, especially in advanced pregnancy
  • Prophylactic antibiotics — a single IV dose at induction of anaesthesia (NICE) → reduce SSI; repeat if the operation outlasts the drug's half-life. A therapeutic course is for perforated or complicated appendicitis, not prophylaxis.
  • Appendix sent for routine histopathology — this detects an appendiceal neoplasm (most often a neuroendocrine/carcinoid tumour). It does not exclude a caecal tumour: that needs interval colonic imaging or colonoscopy.
Special scenarios
  • Appendiceal mass — IV antibiotics and conservative management. Interval appendicectomy is no longer routine; it is reserved for recurrent or persistent symptoms. In older patients arrange interval colonic imaging (CT and/or colonoscopy) to exclude an underlying caecal or appendiceal malignancy.
  • Appendix abscess — IV antibiotics + image-guided percutaneous drainage; urgent appendicectomy is avoided because of the high complication rate, and is reserved for failed conservative treatment.
  • Pelvic abscess — typically days after appendicectomy for a perforated appendix: swinging pyrexia, diarrhoea, tenesmus and mucus per rectum, with a boggy tender mass on PR (not usually palpable abdominally). CT-confirmed; IV antibiotics + image-guided drainage.
  • Antibiotic-only (non-operative) management — an established option for selected adults with uncomplicated appendicitis: no perforation, no abscess, no appendicolith. Appendicectomy remains definitive and is preferred for complicated disease; a substantial minority treated with antibiotics recur within a year and come to surgery, so this belongs in the consent discussion.
Complications
Perforation
  • Peritoneal contamination → generalised peritonitis
  • Especially in children with delayed presentation (>48 h)
  • Signs: sudden pain relief then worsening, rigid abdomen, sepsis
Other complications
  • Appendiceal mass — omentum + small bowel wall off the appendix
  • Pelvic abscess — swinging pyrexia, diarrhoea, tenesmus and mucus PR; boggy tender mass on PR; CT-confirmed; IV abx + image-guided drainage
  • Surgical site infection
  • Stump appendicitis (rare — if insufficient appendix removed)

A classical picture may go straight to theatre, but image the atypical or equivocal patient — and women of childbearing age, children, older patients and pregnancy — to avoid a negative appendicectomy.

USS first-line in women (transabdominal for the appendix + pelvic/TV for the adnexa) and children (avoid radiation). CT if still unclear; MRI in pregnancy. A non-visualised appendix does not exclude appendicitis.

ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRINCIPLES__Pre:
Overview

Pre-operative assessment = identify comorbidities that risk complications during anaesthesia, surgery, or recovery. Timing: far enough before surgery to identify and optimise comorbidities and to complete any further tests or referrals.

Urgency dictates depth: Elective surgery → delay and optimise (e.g. poorly controlled diabetes). Emergency surgery → proceed with whatever optimisation time allows.
Pre-operative History
Systems-based comorbidity sweep
SystemWhat you're screening for / why
CardiovascularHTN; functional capacity — an important part of risk assessment, though subjective assessment alone predicts complications poorly; red-flag undiagnosed disease (exertional chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea)
RespiratoryAssess oxygenation and ventilation; OSA; smoking; can they lie flat and keep still (a practical issue for surgery under spinal anaesthesia). Significant respiratory disease often makes regional anaesthesia preferable to a general anaesthetic. Contraindications to spinal anaesthesia are patient refusal, infection at the puncture site, coagulopathy or anticoagulation, hypovolaemia and fixed cardiac output states
RenalBaseline function + renal-specific meds
EndocrineEsp. diabetes and thyroid disease
FrailtyScore frailty in every patient aged 65 and over — it predicts adverse post-operative outcome independently of ASA grade. A frail patient needs comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimisation before surgery, and a frank discussion of risk
GORDAspiration of gastric contents can be fatal → alters anaesthetic technique
PregnancyOn the day of surgery, sensitively ask every woman of childbearing potential whether she could be pregnant; do a urinary pregnancy test with her consent if there is any doubt, and document the discussion (NICE)

  • Past surgical history — what/when/why; repeat procedures change operative time & difficulty (adhesions)
  • Past anaesthetic history — prior operations, anaesthetic type, any problems
Drug, family & social history
  • Drug history — full list (some need stopping/changing) + drug & non-drug allergies
  • Family history — general + FHx of anaesthetic problems (esp. malignant hyperthermia)
  • Social history — smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs; language/interpreter need; living situation (discharge planning)
Pre-operative Examination & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Mallampati classification — class I (soft palate, uvula, pillars visible) through class IV (only the hard palate visible); a higher class predicts a more difficult laryngoscopy/intubation, though no single bedside test is reliable on its own
NICE: for elective surgery, routine pre-operative tests are not ordered blanket-fashion but are guided by the ASA grade and the severity of surgery (minor / intermediate / major) — e.g. healthy ASA 1 patients for minor surgery need few or no routine tests.
Examination
  • General examination — uncover undiagnosed pathology
  • Airway examination — predict difficulty of airway management (intubation); includes the Mallampati score (I–IV, by how much of the soft palate/uvula is visible on mouth opening — a higher class predicts a more difficult intubation), thyromental distance, mouth opening, neck mobility and dentition. No single bedside test is reliable alone — Mallampati misses about half of difficult airways — so they are combined, and a previous difficult intubation in the anaesthetic history is the strongest predictor of all
  • ± Operation-relevant area if appropriate
Routine investigations
  • MRSA swabs — risk-based, not universal: high-risk pathways (orthopaedic, vascular, cardiothoracic, neurosurgery, any prosthetic implant, critical care) and anyone previously MRSA-positive. Nose + groin/perineum; positive → decolonisation (antiseptic body wash + nasal ointment) before theatre
  • Urine testing — dipstick is not routine (NICE); consider MSU microscopy and culture only if a UTI would change the decision to operate
  • ECG — not routine for a fit ASA 1 patient having minor surgery. Consider in ASA 2 patients having intermediate surgery who have cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity; offer for ASA 3–4 and before major or complex surgery (NICE)
  • CXR — do not routinely offer (NICE); order one only if it will change management

Timing
Far enough ahead to optimise. Urgency dictates depth — elective → optimise; emergency → proceed with available time.
Functional capacity
An important part of risk assessment, but subjective assessment alone is unreliable. CPET measures it objectively (VO₂ max, anaerobic threshold) in high-risk major surgery.
GORD
Aspiration of gastric contents can be fatal → alters anaesthetic technique. Respiratory disease often favours regional over general anaesthesia; contraindications to spinal are refusal, local infection, coagulopathy, hypovolaemia and fixed cardiac output states.
G&S vs cross-match
G&S if blood might be needed. Cross-match if blood will be needed; cross-match after G&S.
Renal function
Kidney function tests are not routine — consider them in anyone at risk of AKI and before major surgery. Reduce or avoid morphine in significant renal impairment.
Malignant hyperthermia
FHx of anaesthetic problems = the key anaesthetic red flag in family history
MRSA swabs — risk-based, not everyone
High-risk pathways and previous MRSA. Nose + groin/perineum. Positive → decolonisation before theatre.
Pregnancy test
Ask every woman of childbearing potential on the day of surgery; test with her consent if there is any doubt, and document it. It is not a test that can be imposed.
ASA grades
I healthy → V moribund. E suffix = emergency. III has substantive functional limitation; IV is a constant threat to life. It describes physical status — it is not itself a risk score.
Frailty
Score frailty in every patient aged 65 and over — it predicts post-operative outcome independently of ASA grade, and a frail patient needs comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimisation before surgery.

Overview — Goals of Pre-operative Management
Pre-operative management optimises the patient's condition before surgery to minimise perioperative risk. It translates findings from pre-operative assessment into action. Key domains: consent, fasting, medication management, DVT prophylaxis, bowel prep, skin prep, and same-day checks.
Consent
Valid consent requires (Mental Capacity Act)
  • Capacity: understand, retain, weigh, communicate decision
  • Voluntary: free from coercion
  • Informed: material risks, benefits, alternatives explained
  • Written consent on Form 1 for an adult with capacity having a procedure under general or regional anaesthesia, or any procedure carrying significant risk (Form 2 = parental consent for a child; Form 3 = procedures where consciousness is not impaired; Form 4 = adult lacking capacity)
  • Surgeon or trainee supervised by surgeon should obtain consent
The Montgomery ruling
  • Patient must be told of ALL material risks — those a reasonable patient would want to know, or that this specific patient would consider significant
  • Replaces the old Bolam standard for consent
  • Surgeon must tailor risk discussion to the individual
  • Document the discussion, not just the signature
Capacity lacking: Act in best interests (MCA). For elective surgery, delay until capacity returns if possible. For emergency, proceed in best interests — consult next of kin (advisory, not legally binding) + document + consider IMCA.
Fasting (NBM) Guidelines

Avoid in gastroparesis and in insulin-treated diabetes, where it may compromise glycaemic control; use in other people with diabetes only where a local protocol allows.

VTE Prophylaxis
All surgical patients must have a VTE risk assessment on admission and after any change in clinical status (NICE). Hospital-acquired VTE is a major cause of preventable death in hospital.
Mechanical prophylaxis
  • Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression, chosen by procedure and patient (NICE). Stockings are contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease, peripheral neuropathy and severe leg oedema, and must be stopped if the skin marks, blisters or discolours
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) — intra-op + post-op until mobile; especially orthopaedic, major abdominal surgery
  • Early mobilisation
  • Adequate hydration
Pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH)
  • Start: 6–12 h post-op (once haemostasis confirmed)
  • Duration: at least 7 days for general surgery; 28 days for major abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery
  • Time doses around neuraxial blocks: do not insert or remove an epidural/spinal catheter within 12 h of a prophylactic LMWH dose, and give the next dose no sooner than 4 h after insertion or removal (epidural haematoma risk)
  • Withhold for active bleeding or platelets <50
  • Renal dose adjustment if eGFR <30 (use unfractionated heparin)
The Department of Health VTE risk assessment tool used in NHS trusts stratifies patients. High-risk factors: malignancy, previous VTE, thrombophilia, immobility, BMI >30, major pelvic/lower limb surgery.
Diabetes Management Perioperatively
General principles
  • Schedule first on the morning list where possible — minimises fasting time
  • Target BM 6–10 mmol/L perioperatively (avoid hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia)
  • Check capillary glucose at least hourly while nil by mouth and perioperatively; check ketones if the patient is unwell or on an SGLT2 inhibitor
  • Involve diabetic specialist nurse / endocrine team
VRIII (Variable Rate Insulin Infusion)
  • Indicated when more than one meal will be missed, control is poor, surgery is an emergency, or a type 1 diabetic has not had their long-acting insulin
  • Run alongside a substrate fluid of 5% glucose + 0.45% NaCl + 0.15% KCl, and continue the long-acting insulin alongside it
  • Plain 0.9% saline is not used because it gives no glucose substrate (hypoglycaemia and ketosis) and no potassium, which insulin drives into cells
  • Monitor BM hourly on VRIII; electrolytes 4–6 hourly
  • Convert back to S/C insulin at the first meal — give the subcutaneous dose with the meal and continue the VRIII for a further 30–60 min before stopping, or a type 1 diabetic will become ketotic
Bowel Preparation & Skin Prep
Bowel prep
  • Routine mechanical bowel prep NOT recommended for most colorectal surgery (ERAS / NICE evidence: no mortality/anastomotic leak benefit, causes dehydration)
  • Still used for: left colonic anastomoses (some centres), rectal surgery, laparoscopic colectomy with intra-op colonoscopy
  • All colorectal cases receive IV antibiotic prophylaxis at induction
Skin prep & SSI prevention
  • Chlorhexidine 2% in 70% alcohol — superior to povidone-iodine for SSI prevention (NICE)
  • Prophylactic IV antibiotics at induction, before skin incision — earlier if a tourniquet is to be used. A single dose suffices for most operations; repeat only for long procedures or major blood loss, and do not prescribe a routine post-operative course
  • Hair removal: clippers NOT razor (razors cause micro-abrasions → ↑SSI)
  • Maintain normothermia (warm air blanket, warm IV fluids)
  • Maintain normoglycaemia (↑glucose → ↑SSI risk)
ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery)
Multimodal protocol across pre-, intra-, and post-operative phases. Reduces complications, length of stay, and costs. Now standard for colorectal, orthopaedic, and major abdominal surgery.
Pre-operative ERAS elements
  • Patient education and goal-setting
  • Prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, smoking cessation)
  • Carbohydrate loading (as above)
  • Avoid prolonged fasting / bowel prep
  • Anaemia correction — screen for and treat anaemia before elective surgery. Confirm iron deficiency (ferritin, transferrin saturation), then oral iron if there is time before surgery, or IV iron if surgery is soon or oral iron is not tolerated or effective
  • VTE prophylaxis planning
Intra/post-operative ERAS elements
  • Short-acting anaesthetic agents
  • Laparoscopic approach where possible
  • Goal-directed fluid therapy (avoid over/under-hydration)
  • Epidural / regional anaesthesia to reduce opioids
  • Early feeding (day of surgery or day 1)
  • Early mobilisation
  • Avoid NGT, urinary catheter, drains if not required

Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution (third-spacing, sepsis, liver failure) and Reassessment. Resuscitation, replacement and maintenance are the three you prescribe; redistribution and reassessment shape how you adjust.

  • Patient is in shock / hypovolaemia
  • Rapid isotonic bolus to restore perfusion

  • Patient has ongoing abnormal losses (vomiting, NG, stoma, diarrhoea)
  • Maintenance ± adjustments for deficits and losses

📷 Image placeholder — IM adrenaline injection site in anaphylaxis — the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh; the 500 microgram (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, 1 in 1000) dose is given here first
IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) → massive mast cell degranulation → histamine, tryptase → ↓SVR + bronchospasm + ↑vascular permeability. Triggers: drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs), foods (nuts), latex, stings.
Clinical features
Presentation
  • Skin: urticaria, erythema, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat)
  • Airway: stridor, hoarseness (laryngeal oedema)
  • Breathing: bronchospasm, wheeze, ↑RR
  • Circulation: tachycardia, ↓BP, warm flushed skin
  • ± nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps
Management (Resuscitation Council UK)
  • Remove trigger
  • IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh — FIRST
  • Lie the patient flat with legs raised (semi-recumbent if breathing is the dominant problem, but still with legs raised). Do not sit or stand them up, even if they feel better — a sudden change of posture can precipitate cardiac arrest
  • Repeat at 5 min if no improvement
  • If still not responding after 2 appropriate IM doses this is refractory anaphylaxis — give further IV fluid and call critical care/anaesthetics urgently for an adrenaline infusion. Do not give IV adrenaline boluses outside specialist settings
  • High-flow O₂; call 999/crash team
  • IV fluid bolus 500 mL – 1 L crystalloid
  • Antihistamine — no longer part of initial emergency care; a non-sedating oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine) may be given after stabilisation for persistent skin symptoms (RCUK)
  • Corticosteroids — no longer routinely recommended in acute anaphylaxis (RCUK)
  • Observation before discharge is risk-stratified from resolution of symptoms (NICE): minimum 2 h if low risk (single dose, full resolution, already carrying and trained on an auto-injector, good access to care); minimum 6 h if 2 doses were needed or there is a history of biphasic reaction; minimum 12 h if >2 doses were needed, severe respiratory compromise or severe asthma, possible ongoing allergen absorption, or difficult access to emergency care
  • Discharge with two adrenaline auto-injectors, training in the specific device, a written emergency plan, and referral to a specialist allergy service (NICE)
Serum tryptase: ideally three samples — as soon as feasible once treatment has started (never delay resuscitation to take blood), a second 1–2 h after symptom onset (no later than 4 h), and a baseline at least 24 h later. A rise and fall confirms mast cell activation. Send to immunology.
Cardiogenic Shock
Most commonly from acute anterior STEMI (LV pump failure). Mortality is high. Paradox: giving fluids may worsen pulmonary oedema.
Diagnosis
  • SBP <90 mmHg AND CO/CI reduced AND adequate filling pressure
  • Cold, clammy, ↑JVP, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles
  • ECG: STEMI, new LBBB
  • Echo: confirms low EF, wall motion abnormality
  • Troponin ↑, BNP ↑
Management
  • Revascularisation ASAP — primary PCI if MI; this is the definitive treatment
  • Vasopressors: noradrenaline (MAP ≥65) ± dobutamine (inotrope)
  • Avoid fluids if pulmonary oedema present
  • Furosemide if fluid overloaded
  • Refer early to cardiology and ICU — mechanical circulatory support is a specialist-centre decision
  • ICU admission
Obstructive Shock

📷 Image placeholder — cardiac tamponade on echocardiography — a large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium/ventricle
In obstructive shock, fluids help temporise (maintain preload) but treat the cause immediately — the obstruction must be relieved. Fluids without relief = futile.
Neurogenic Shock
Spinal cord injury above T6 → loss of sympathetic tone → massive vasodilation. Unique: hypotension + BRADYCARDIA (not tachycardia — unlike all other shocks). Treat with vasopressors (noradrenaline/phenylephrine) + IV fluids + immobilise spine.

Do not confuse this with spinal shock, which is a neurological, not a circulatory, phenomenon — transient flaccid paralysis, sensory loss and areflexia below the injury level, resolving over days to weeks into spasticity and hyperreflexia.

ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRINCIPLES__Abd:
Overview

A hernia is an organ or its fascia protruding outside the walls of its usual cavity. Inguinal hernias account for 75% of all abdominal hernias.

The two decisive forks
  • Is it complicated? Reducible & wide-necked → safe-ish. Irreducible / narrow-necked → incarceration → obstruction and/or strangulation. The stages usually run in that order but not always: in a Richter's hernia only part of the bowel circumference is trapped, so the lumen stays open and it can strangulate and perforate without ever obstructing.
  • Which anatomical type? Each defined by where it emerges
Cross-references
  • Bowel obstruction — hernia is a top-3 cause
  • GORD — hiatus hernia
  • Stomas — parastomal hernia
Presentation & Examination
Typical presentation
  • Soft lump through abdominal wall
  • Reducible — pushes back on lying down or gentle pressure
  • Protrudes on coughing (↑ intra-abdominal pressure) or standing (gravity)
  • Aching / dragging sensation
Examining a groin lump — structured check
  • Cough impulse (irreducible hernia may lose this)
  • Location relative to pubic tubercle — the key discriminator
  • Reducible on lying down / gentle pressure?
  • If entering scrotum — can you get above it / separate from testis?
The single highest-yield discriminator: Inguinal = superomedial to the pubic tubercle. Femoral = inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
📷 Image placeholder — groin hernia landmarks — the pubic tubercle as the reference point, with an inguinal hernia emerging superomedial to it and a femoral hernia inferolateral to it
Complications — The Deterioration Ladder
Neck width drives risk: Wide neck = reduces easily, lower risk. Narrow neck = high risk — bowel gets trapped and cannot decompress.
StageWhat happensPresentation
IncarcerationIrreducible — bowel trapped in the sac, cannot be reducedFirm, tender lump that won't reduce; precursor to below
ObstructionTrapped bowel blocks faecal flowVomiting, generalised pain, absolute constipation
StrangulationNeck cuts off blood supply → ischaemia → infarction. Can occur without obstruction (Richter's hernia)Irreducible + tender, with overlying skin changes, tachycardia, fever or peritonism — surgical emergency (infarcts within hours). Do not attempt to reduce it
Management
Three options
  • Conservative (watchful waiting) — the default for an asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in a man; repair is offered if it becomes symptomatic, irreducible, or limits normal work or activity. Not an option for femoral hernias
  • Tension-free repair (preferred) — mesh placed over the defect, sutured to surrounding tissue; tissue ingrowth reinforces it. Open mesh repair is standard for a primary unilateral inguinal hernia; laparoscopic repair is an option for all and is preferred for bilateral and recurrent hernias (NICE)
  • Tension repair — sutures pull defect edges together; rarely used (painful, high recurrence)
Strangulation = emergency
  • Do not attempt to reduce a hernia that is irreducible and tender, or has overlying skin changes or systemic upset — forcing ischaemic bowel back into the abdomen risks perforation with the source of sepsis now unmonitorable
  • Resuscitate: IV access, fluids, analgesia, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics if septic → immediate surgical assessment and theatre
  • Emergency surgery — resect ischaemic / necrotic bowel
  • All femoral hernias are repaired surgically, and urgently (narrow rigid ring → high strangulation risk; a large minority present already obstructed or strangulated). Because inguinal and femoral hernias cannot be told apart reliably at the bedside, refer any groin hernia in a woman urgently
Inguinal Hernias (75% of all abdominal wall hernias; the great majority in men)

  • Deep ring landmark: midpoint ASIS → pubic tubercle

  • Children: an inguinal hernia at any age needs surgical referral and prompt repair — watchful waiting is not appropriate, and the incarceration risk is highest under 6 months. A tender, irreducible groin/scrotal lump in an infant is an emergency, alongside testicular torsion
Femoral Hernias — Always Repair
Through the femoral canal, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. Commoner in women (esp. multiparous). The femoral ring has narrow, rigid borders → high strangulation risk → all femoral hernias are repaired surgically.
Femoral canal borders — F-L-I-P

Stomach herniates through the diaphragm into the thorax. Widening of the normally narrow, fixed hiatus disrupts the LOS → reflux.

ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRINCIPLES__Pos:
Overview
Complications can follow even simple surgery. The examined skill is early recognition — haemorrhage and sepsis especially, as patients can deteriorate within hours. Two organising axes: by system (respiratory, cardiovascular, GI, urinary, wound, haematological) and by timing (immediate → early → late). The post-operative pyrexia timeline is the highest-yield application.
Post-operative Pyrexia — The 5 Ws
The principle: timing of fever narrows the differential before you examine the patient. Early fever = respiratory; later fever = wound / VTE / collection.
Timing"W"CauseKey action
Day 0–2WindThe systemic inflammatory response to surgery itself (commonest); early pneumonia or aspiration. Atelectasis is common but does not itself cause feverLook for a treatable cause before labelling it; analgesia, chest physio, mobilise, deep breathing (these treat the atelectasis, not the fever)
Day 3–5WaterUTI (catheter-associated)Urine dip/MSU, remove catheter early
Day 4–6WalkingDVT / PEDoppler USS leg, CTPA; LMWH + TEDs
Day 5–7WoundSSI, anastomotic leakInspect wound, examine abdomen, bloods + CT
Any timeWonder drugs / What's in the lineDrug reaction, transfusion reaction, line/cannula sepsisReview drug chart, change/remove lines, blood cultures
Haemorrhage — The Immediate Emergency
Bleeding into a drain, internally as a haematoma, or from the wound → untreated leads to hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia, ↓BP, pale/clammy). Recognise fast — BP is maintained until Class III (>1.5 L lost).
TypeTimingMechanism
PrimaryIntra-operativeBleeding during surgery from a vessel
ReactiveWithin 24 hSlipped ligature or missed vessel as BP normalises post-op
Secondary7–10 daysInfection erodes a vessel — often presents as sudden haemorrhage into a previously healing wound
Management: resuscitate (large-bore IV ×2, bloods, cross-match, IV fluids/blood), identify bleeding source, urgent surgical review. Secondary haemorrhage = infection control + surgical re-exploration.
Respiratory Complications
Atelectasis (Day 0–2)
  • Collapse of lung segments due to under-ventilation (pain → shallow breathing → mucous plugging)
  • Atelectasis is common but does not cause fever — the classic teaching is not supported by the evidence. A fever in the first 48 h is usually the systemic inflammatory response to surgery itself, and is a diagnosis of exclusion: still look for early pneumonia or aspiration, a transfusion or drug reaction, line sepsis and, within 24–48 h, a necrotising surgical site infection
  • Presents: ↑RR, ↓SpO₂, reduced air entry at bases
  • CXR: basal shadowing
  • Management: adequate analgesia (allows deep breathing), chest physiotherapy, mobilisation, incentive spirometry
Pneumonia
  • Hospital-acquired (HAP) — gram-negative organisms common
  • Presents: fever, productive cough, ↑WCC, consolidation on CXR
  • Management: sputum culture, antibiotics per local protocol, O₂, physio
  • Risk ↑ with: prolonged ventilation, aspiration (dysphagia, NGT), immunosuppression
The analgesia link: adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation → reduces atelectasis → reduces pneumonia. Under-treated pain → shallow breathing → retained secretions → infection.
Cardiovascular & Thromboembolic Complications
VTE — DVT & PE (Day 4–6)
  • DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, erythema
  • PE: pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, ↑HR, hypoxia; massive PE → haemodynamic collapse
  • Investigations: go straight to imaging — Doppler USS (DVT), CTPA (PE). D-dimer is unhelpful post-operatively, because surgery itself raises it
  • Prevention: LMWH + anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression + early mobilisation; 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery
  • Treatment: apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line (NICE); therapeutic LMWH where a DOAC is unsuitable or reversibility matters immediately post-op
Cardiac complications
  • Arrhythmias — especially new AF (surgery triggers sympathetic activation + hypoxia + electrolyte disturbance)
  • ACS / MI — surgical stress unmasks coronary disease; most occur in the first 48 hours. The majority are silent: chest pain is masked by analgesia, so the presentation is often unexplained hypotension, tachycardia, new AF, breathlessness or confusion. Low threshold for ECG + troponin in a high-risk patient who deteriorates without an obvious cause
  • Stroke — embolic (AF, air embolus) or haemorrhagic (hypertension post-op)
  • Risk ↑ in: pre-existing cardiac disease, major vascular surgery, emergency operations
Gastrointestinal Complications
📷 Image placeholder — abdominal X-ray of post-operative ileus — gas-filled dilated loops of bowel throughout both small and large bowel (uniform dilatation), in contrast to mechanical obstruction where distended proximal loops give way to a collapsed distal bowel
Post-operative ileus
  • Functional bowel dysmotility — not mechanical obstruction
  • Common after abdominal/pelvic surgery, long anaesthetics, opioids, electrolyte disturbance
  • Presents: abdominal distension, vomiting, absent bowel sounds, no flatus or stool
  • AXR: dilated loops throughout (vs obstruction — dilated proximal, decompressed distal)
  • Distinguishing from mechanical obstruction: ileus gives a silent abdomen with absent bowel sounds; mechanical obstruction gives high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds and colicky pain. AXR is suggestive, not definitive — if the ileus has not settled by day 3–4, or the patient deteriorates, get a CT with contrast to exclude mechanical obstruction, a collection or a leak
  • Management: IV fluids, correct electrolytes especially K⁺, mobilise, minimise opioids. An NG tube is for symptomatic relief where there is significant distension and vomiting with aspiration risk — it does not hasten resolution, and routine NG decompression is avoided in ERAS. Encourage early oral intake as tolerated
Anastomotic leak (classically day 5–7, but anywhere from day 2 to day 14)
  • Breakdown of a bowel join → GI contents into peritoneum
  • Presents: increasing pain, fever, peritonism, sepsis — but that is the late picture
  • Red flag: unexplained persistent tachycardia, new-onset AF, oliguria, prolonged ileus or simple "failure to progress" in a patient who otherwise looks well. Unexplained tachycardia or new AF after bowel surgery is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise — do not put it down to pain or dehydration
  • Drain output becomes faeculent / turbid; CRP rises sharply on day 3–5
  • CT abdomen (with contrast) — confirms leak + free gas/fluid
  • Management: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, urgent senior surgical review and CT with contrast. A small contained leak in a stable patient may be managed with radiologically-guided drainage; peritonitis, sepsis or a large leak needs urgent re-operation (washout, defunctioning stoma ± takedown of the anastomosis)
📷 Image placeholder — contrast CT of an anastomotic leak — extraluminal free gas and fluid collection adjacent to the bowel anastomosis, with contrast leaking from the lumen
Late GI complications
  • Adhesions → small bowel obstruction (most common cause of SBO in adults)
  • Incisional hernia → protrusion through the scar (esp. midline laparotomy); risk ↑ with: obesity, infection, poor nutrition, steroids
  • Constipation — opioids + immobility; prescribe laxatives with opioids routinely
Wound Complications
📷 Image placeholder — burst abdomen (wound dehiscence / evisceration) — full-thickness separation of a midline laparotomy wound with loops of bowel/omentum protruding through the skin; a surgical emergency preceded by serosanguineous "pink fluid" leak
Surgical site infection (most often day 5–10; by definition within 30 days, or longer with an implant)
  • Erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, wound pain ± systemic sepsis
  • Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus is commonest overall (skin flora); after bowel surgery expect Gram-negatives (E. coli) and anaerobes. A wound infection appearing in the first 24–48 h with pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapidly spreading erythema suggests a necrotising infection — a surgical emergency, not a course of oral antibiotics
  • Superficial: skin/subcutaneous tissue; deep: fascia/muscle; organ/space (e.g. intra-abdominal abscess)
  • Management: wound swab, open and drain superficial infections, antibiotics for systemic features
  • Prevention: chlorhexidine skin prep, prophylactic antibiotics at induction, normothermia, normoglycaemia
Wound dehiscence / Burst abdomen
  • Dehiscence: partial separation of wound edges
  • Burst abdomen (evisceration): full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding through skin — surgical emergency
  • Warning sign: serosanguineous "pink fluid" draining from wound (day 5–10)
  • Management: cover the wound and any protruding bowel with saline-soaked sterile gauze; nil by mouth, IV access, IV fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, NG tube; urgent senior surgical review and return to theatre for washout and mass closure with non-absorbable sutures
  • Risk ↑: obesity, malnutrition, infection, steroids, poor surgical technique, coughing
Urinary Complications
UTI (Day 3–5)
  • Catheter-associated UTI — a common healthcare-associated infection post-op, and the great majority are catheter-related
  • Dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine ± systemic sepsis
  • Investigations: urine dip, MSU + culture
  • Management: antibiotics per local protocol, remove catheter as soon as possible
Urinary retention & AKI
  • Retention: common post-op (opioids, spinal anaesthesia, pelvic surgery); ♂ > ♀ (BPH risk); trial without catheter (TWOC) needed
  • Confirm retention with a bedside bladder scan before catheterising — this avoids unnecessary catheters and the CAUTIs they cause. In an older patient, retention may present only as delirium
  • AKI: hypovolaemia, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, gentamicin, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, contrast) → oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) → rising creatinine. Identify and treat the cause: stop or withhold nephrotoxics and review the whole drug chart, exclude obstruction (bladder scan; flush or replace a blocked catheter), treat sepsis, and give a fluid challenge if hypovolaemic. Monitor UO and U&Es, and check for hyperkalaemia
Recognising the Deteriorating Patient — Sepsis
Every complication in this topic — leak, SSI, catheter-associated UTI, line sepsis, pneumonia — can kill through septic deterioration. Score NEWS2 on every set of observations and escalate on a rising score; a post-operative patient whose NEWS2 climbs has a complication until proven otherwise.
  • Assess A–E, take blood cultures and lactate, give oxygen to target, IV fluids and antibiotics, and monitor urine output (the "give 3, take 3" of the Sepsis Six)
  • Antibiotic urgency is set by NEWS2 (NICE): broad-spectrum antibiotics and infection-specific tests within 1 h if NEWS2 ≥7, 3 h if NEWS2 5–6, 6 h if NEWS2 1–4 — clarifying the diagnosis and targeting therapy in the lower-risk groups
  • Antibiotics do not achieve source control. Escalate to the surgical team in parallel: theatre or radiological drainage is what treats the cause
  • New diarrhoea after surgery: think Clostridioides difficile — these patients have had antibiotics, opioids and PPIs. Send a stool sample, isolate the patient, stop or narrow the precipitating antibiotic, review the PPI, and involve microbiology
Systemic Complications
Anaemia
  • Post-op FBC at 24–48 h; causes: intra-op blood loss, haemodilution, haemolysis
  • Investigate the cause; treat iron-deficiency anaemia with oral or IV iron (NICE) rather than transfusing
  • Hb <70 g/L → blood transfusion, target 70–90 g/L; <80 g/L with a target of 80–100 g/L in acute coronary syndrome (NICE)
  • Jehovah's Witnesses: may refuse transfusion by valid advance directive — respect autonomy if capacity present; optimise pre-op, use cell salvage, minimise intra-op loss
Post-op nausea & vomiting (PONV)
  • Risk factors (Apfel score): female, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness, post-op opioids (each = 1 point; score ≥3 = high risk)
  • Prophylaxis: ondansetron + dexamethasone at induction (± cyclizine) in high-risk; use TIVA (propofol) instead of volatile agents
  • Treatment: ondansetron 4 mg IV/IM, or cyclizine 50 mg IV. Metoclopramide 10 mg IV is an option but is a prokinetic — avoid it in the first 3–4 days after bowel surgery with an anastomosis, and in obstruction or perforation; it is restricted to short-term use (maximum 5 days) because of extrapyramidal side effects (MHRA)
Post-operative delirium
  • Acute fluctuating confusion — common in elderly/frail post-op
  • Reversible causes (PINCH ME): Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment
  • Exclude: hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention, hypoglycaemia
  • Screen with the 4AT. Delirium is under-recognised, particularly the hypoactive (quiet, withdrawn) form, which is commoner than the agitated form
  • Management: identify and treat the cause. Non-pharmacological measures first — reorientation, familiar staff and faces, glasses and hearing aids, daylight and sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, treat pain and constipation. Only if the patient is distressed or a risk to themselves or others and de-escalation has failed, consider short-term (usually ≤1 week) haloperidol at the lowest effective dose (NICE) — avoid in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia. Avoid benzodiazepines, which worsen delirium — the exception is alcohol withdrawal, where they are the treatment
Nutrition post-op
  • Enteral preferred (oral → NG/PEG → jejunostomy)
  • Early feeding (day of surgery in ERAS) reduces infective complications + ileus + LOS
  • TPN via central line only if GI tract completely unusable — hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins
  • Screen with MUST; dietitian if complex needs
Analgesia & Procedural Support
Analgesic ladder (multimodal)
  • Step 1: regular paracetamol 1 g QDS
  • Step 2: add an NSAID (ibuprofen or naproxen) — avoid in: renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, established cardiovascular disease and heart failure, and in anyone with previous NSAID or aspirin hypersensitivity (ask about this specifically in asthmatics). Systemic diclofenac is contraindicated in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease and moderate-to-severe heart failure (MHRA), so it is not a good default post-operative choice
  • Step 3: add weak opioid (codeine, tramadol) or strong opioid (morphine, oxycodone)
  • Prescribe laxatives with all opioids (prevent opioid-induced constipation). It is reducing the opioid load with multimodal and regional analgesia that reduces ileus, not laxatives
  • Regional techniques (epidural, nerve block) reduce systemic opioid requirements
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
  • IV opioid on-demand with lockout interval
  • Only the patient presses the button — safety mechanism; staff/family must not press it
  • Have naloxone available (respiratory depression), antiemetic (PONV), atropine (bradycardia)
  • Review daily — wean when oral intake re-established
Lines, tubes & drains — remove early (ERAS principle)
  • Urinary catheter: remove when mobile + no urological indication → TWOC; retention risk in males
  • Drains: remove when output <30 mL/24 h (or per surgeon — drain removal timing is contested)
  • IV cannulae: inspect daily for phlebitis (VIP score) and re-site when clinically indicated — routine replacement at a fixed interval is no longer recommended; remove as soon as IV access is no longer needed
  • NGT: remove when GI function returns and oral intake adequate
  • Every device left in longer than needed ↑ infection risk and impairs mobilisation
⭐ Exam Pearls
5 Ws pyrexia timeline
Wind (0–2) → Water (3–5) → Walking (4–6) → Wound (5–7) → Wonder drugs/line (any time)
Day 0–2 fever ≠ atelectasis
Atelectasis is common post-op but does not cause fever. Early fever is usually the surgical inflammatory response — exclude early pneumonia/aspiration, transfusion or drug reaction, line sepsis and necrotising SSI. Analgesia + physio + mobilisation still treat the atelectasis.
Haemorrhage: primary/reactive/secondary
Reactive = <24 h (slipped ligature). Secondary = 7–10 d (infection erodes vessel).
Ileus = functional, not mechanical
Silent abdomen (vs tinkling in obstruction); dilated loops throughout on AXR. IV fluids + correct K⁺. No surgery for the ileus itself — but if it has not settled by day 3–4, CT to exclude obstruction or a leak.
Anastomotic leak ~Day 5–7 (range day 2–14)
The exam trap is the patient who looks well but has unexplained tachycardia or new AF — that is a leak until proven otherwise. CRP spikes day 3–5. CT with contrast confirms. Resuscitate, antibiotics, urgent surgical review.
Burst abdomen = emergency
Pink fluid from the wound = warning sign. Saline-soaked gauze over the bowel, nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics → theatre urgently.
PONV Apfel score
Female + non-smoker + prior PONV + post-op opioids. ≥3 = high risk. Prophylaxis: ondansetron + dex.
NSAIDs: avoid in asthma, renal, cardiac, ulcers
Multimodal analgesia reduces opioid need — combine paracetamol + NSAID + opioid step-wise.
PCA: only patient presses
Have naloxone + antiemetic + atropine available. Never press for the patient.
Anaemia thresholds
Hb <100 → oral/IV iron. Hb <70 → transfuse (<80 in acute coronary syndrome). Respect Jehovah's Witness advance directive.
Delirium: PINCH ME
Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment. Treat cause first.
Remove everything early (ERAS)
Catheter, drain, NGT, cannula — each device left in longer than needed ↑ infection + impairs mobilisation.

Drug Details
Paracetamol
  • MOA: inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis (COX)
  • Safe in renal failure, pregnancy, elderly
  • Hepatotoxic in overdose (N-acetylcysteine antidote)
  • IV paracetamol: rapid onset, useful peri-operatively
NSAIDs
  • MOA: inhibit COX-1/2 → ↓prostaglandin synthesis
  • Contraindications: peptic ulcer disease, CKD (↓GFR), HF, asthma (aspirin-sensitive), pregnancy (3rd trimester), warfarin use
  • SE: GI ulceration (give PPI cover), fluid retention, AKI
Opioids
  • Morphine: oral (IR for breakthrough, MR for regular) or IV. Gold standard strong opioid.
  • SE: N&V, constipation (always prescribe laxatives), sedation, respiratory depression, urinary retention
  • Antidote: naloxone (opioid antagonist) 0.4mg IV/IM — reverses all effects
  • Fentanyl: patch or IV. Preferred in renal failure.
  • Tramadol: weak opioid + noradrenaline/serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Seizure risk.
Adjuvants
  • Neuropathic pain: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin
  • Bone pain: NSAIDs + bisphosphonates
  • Opioid-sparing: ketamine (NMDA antagonist), clonidine
  • Regional: nerve blocks, epidurals (opioid + local anaesthetic)
Local Anaesthetics

Block sodium channels → prevent nerve depolarisation. Duration: lidocaine 1–2h, bupivacaine 4–8h. Max doses are critical.

💊
Lidocaine
Max 3mg/kg plain · 7mg/kg with adrenaline. Fast onset, medium duration. Used for infiltration, nerve blocks, IV regional.
💊
Bupivacaine
Max 2mg/kg. Long-acting. Used for epidurals, spinals, nerve blocks. Most cardiotoxic.
LA Toxicity
Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → cardiovascular collapse. Treat: intralipid 20% (lipid emulsion) IV + resuscitation.
⭐ Exam Pearls
WHO ladder: regular paracetamol ± NSAIDs → add weak opioid → add strong opioid. Always prescribe laxatives with opioids.
NSAIDs contraindicated in: CKD, peptic ulcer, HF, 3rd trimester pregnancy, aspirin-sensitive asthma.
Naloxone: reverses all opioid effects including analgesia — titrate carefully to avoid precipitating pain.
Morphine in renal failure: accumulation of active metabolite (morphine-6-glucuronide) → use fentanyl instead.
LA toxicity: lipid emulsion (intralipid 20%) is antidote — lipid sink for LA molecules.
Bupivacaine: most cardiotoxic LA. Lidocaine: must not exceed 3mg/kg without adrenaline.

Overview — "If the gut works, use it"

The decisive fork governing every nutritional decision: choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate.

RouteUse whenRequires working gut?
Oral supportPatient can swallow safelyYes
Enteral (tube)Unsafe/inadequate oral intake but functional GI tractYes
Parenteral (IV)GI tract non-functional, inaccessible, or perforatedNo
Screening & Defining Malnutrition (NICE)
Screen all inpatients on admission and outpatients at first appointment. Repeat weekly for inpatients. Tool = MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool).
Malnourished — any one of:
  • BMI <18.5
  • Unintentional weight loss >10% in 3–6 months
  • BMI <20 + weight loss >5% in 3–6 months
At risk — any of:
  • Eaten little/nothing for >5 days (or likely to for next 5+)
  • Poor absorption or high losses
  • Increased needs from catabolism
Daily targets (not severely ill, no refeeding risk)
  • Energy: 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25)
  • Protein: 0.8–1.5 g/kg
  • Fluid: 30–35 mL/kg (+ extra for drains/fistulae)
  • Plus: electrolytes, minerals, micronutrients, fibre
  • Seriously ill / >5 days nil intake: start at ≤50% of target for first 1–2 days, then build up
Enteral Tube Feeding
📷 Image placeholder — enteral feeding tube routes — nasogastric (NG) and nasojejunal (NJ) tubes passed via the nose, and percutaneous PEG (into the stomach) and PEJ/jejunostomy (into the jejunum) tubes through the abdominal wall; post-pyloric routes (NJ/PEJ) bypass the stomach to reduce aspiration
Indication — both must hold: (1) inadequate or unsafe oral intake AND (2) functional, accessible GI tract.
RouteSiteUse whenKey points
NGStomach (nasal)Short-term (<4 weeks)Most common; allows bolus + hypertonic feeds; easily displaced
NJJejunum (nasal)Short-term + delayed gastric emptying / reflux riskReduces aspiration risk; post-pyloric placement can be difficult
PEGStomach (percutaneous)Long-term (≥4 weeks)Stroke, MND, Parkinson's, oesophageal cancer; placed endoscopically under antibiotic cover; usable 4 h after insertion
PEJ / jejunostomyJejunum (percutaneous)Long-term + high reflux/aspiration riskPermits early post-op feeding; more technically demanding
The 4-week rule: <4 weeks → NG. ≥4 weeks → consider PEG. The single most-tested route rule.
NG safety (NPSA): Confirm position after placement and before every use — aspirate pH ≤5.5 on pH paper. X-ray if pH equivocal. Misplaced NG into the lung is a Never Event.
Parenteral Nutrition
Access — duration drives the line
  • <14 days, no other central need → peripheral venous catheter (mind pH/tonicity)
  • <30 days → non-tunnelled central catheter
  • >30 days (long-term) → tunnelled subclavian line

TPN typically via central line — hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins.

PN complications
  • Line sepsis — the big one; daily catheter-site inspection
  • Thrombosis
  • Refeeding syndrome (see below)
  • Deranged LFTs / cholestasis
  • Electrolyte and glucose disturbance

Trophic feeding — keep minimal enteral feeding alongside PN where possible → maintains gut function, reduces cholestasis.

Refeeding Syndrome — High-Yield Complication
📷 Image placeholder — refeeding syndrome mechanism — a carbohydrate load drives an insulin surge that pushes phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly (↓ serum phosphate is cardinal) and raises thiamine demand, risking arrhythmias, cardiac/respiratory failure and seizures
Mechanism: Carbohydrate load → insulin surge → rapid intracellular electrolyte shift → ↓ phosphate (cardinal), ↓ K⁺, ↓ Mg²⁺ + expanding ECF volume. Thiamine demand spikes. Consequences: cardiac/respiratory failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, coma.
High-risk criteria (NICE)
One of these aloneOr two of these
BMI <16BMI <18.5
Weight loss >15% in 3–6 monthsWeight loss >10%
Little/no intake >10 daysLittle/no intake >5 days
Low K⁺/PO₄³⁻/Mg²⁺ before feedingAlcohol or drug history (incl. insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics)
Prevention & management (NICE)
  • Start at max 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, BMI <14)
  • Build to full needs over 4–7 days
  • Thiamine 200–300 mg/day + vitamin B co strong — before and during the first 10 days
  • Replace K⁺, PO₄³⁻, Mg²⁺ as needed; do not pre-correct electrolytes before starting feeding
Enteral Feeding Complications & Monitoring
Enteral complications
  • Tube-related: NG — discomfort, sinusitis, erosions; bronchial misplacement (fatal if used); PEG — stoma infection, peritonitis, dislodgement
  • Blockage — flush with water before and after every use
  • Infection — discard feed sets every 24 h
  • Aspiration — nurse at ≥30° during and after feeding; post-pyloric tubes for flat patients
  • GI symptoms — bloating, diarrhoea, nausea; slow rate or switch to continuous feed
Monitoring
  • Bloods (daily until stable): U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate; LFTs/INR, calcium, albumin, CRP
  • Trace elements (Zn, Cu, Se) periodically on long-term PN
  • Clinical: weight, BMI, fluid balance, GI tolerance, tube/stoma site
  • NG: pH check before every feed
  • PN lines: daily site inspection for infection
Ethics & End of Life — CANH
Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration (CANH) is a medical treatment — not basic care. It can be withheld or withdrawn like any treatment, using the same consent framework. Capacity drives the decision: competent patient's refusal must be respected. If they lack capacity, decide in best interests (advance directives, MDT, family).
